overview.text: Plague is an infectious disease of humans and other mammals caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which circulates naturally among wild rodents and their fleas. People most often become infected through flea bites, but contact with infected animal tissue and inhaling droplets from an infected animal or person can also spread it. Its forms include bubonic plague, which typically causes painful swollen lymph nodes called buboes; septicemic plague, which infects the bloodstream; and pneumonic plague, which affects the lungs. Only pneumonic plague is known to spread person to person through infectious respiratory droplets. Historically, plague was known as the Black Death during the fourteenth century. Antibiotics can treat plague when it is diagnosed promptly.

key_facts.text: Yersinia pestis circulates naturally among rodents and their fleas; infected flea bites are the most common way people get plague.
Bubonic plague commonly causes a tender, swollen lymph node called a bubo.
The main forms include bubonic, septicemic (bloodstream), and pneumonic (lung) plague.
Pneumonic plague can spread between people through infectious respiratory droplets; other forms are not spread person to person.
Plague was known as the Black Death during the fourteenth century, and antibiotics can be effective when treatment begins early.
